title: Research Explained #26 — Can Two Devices Create a Shortcut Through Spacetime?
html:
Two Devices, One Extraordinary Question

Imagine placing one device near Earth and another near a distant star.

Now imagine that these devices could somehow cooperate to create a connection between their locations.

A spacecraft enters near the first device and emerges near the second. It never exceeds the speed of light in its immediate surroundings, yet the journey takes far less time than light would require to cross the ordinary distance between the stars.

Could physics permit something like this?

The question is worth exploring because general relativity allows spacetime to have geometry that is far more interesting than the flat, familiar picture we usually imagine.

But there is a critical distinction between asking whether such a connection can be described mathematically and establishing that two physical devices could create one.

At Beyond the Light Barrier, we want to investigate the question without assuming the answer.

We are not proposing that such devices exist, that they can be built, or that a particular wormhole or warp-drive model provides the solution.

We are asking what physics would require.

1. What Would Count as a Shortcut?

Suppose two stars are separated by ten light-years.

In an approximately stationary, weakly curved region of space, light traveling along the ordinary route would take approximately ten years, as measured in the reference frame in which that distance is defined.

A spacecraft following the same route at less than the speed of light would take longer.

But general relativity allows us to ask a different question:

Could spacetime contain another route between the two locations?

A familiar analogy is a sheet of paper.

Draw two dots far apart on the sheet. Traveling along the surface between them takes a certain distance.

If the sheet could be folded so that the dots nearly touched, a connection between them might offer a shorter route.

This is a useful illustration, but it has a limitation.

Spacetime does not need to fold into a higher-dimensional room for general relativity to describe unusual connections. What matters is the geometry and topology of spacetime itself.

And a drawing of a shortcut does not establish that the shortcut can exist physically.

The clock matters more than the drawing

To determine whether a proposed route really provides faster travel, we must specify who measures the journey and how the clocks are compared.

In curved spacetime, distance and elapsed time depend on the geometry and the observers involved.

We cannot establish faster-than-light travel simply by drawing a short path or reporting a large coordinate speed.

Start both comparisons from the same identified departure event. Compare the arrivals on the destination station’s clock, and say which route the light follows. A craft can beat light sent along a longer route. Within one spacetime it cannot beat the earliest causal arrival at that station. To claim an advance over the spacetime without the shortcut, compare against the earliest light arrival in a reference geometry with physically matched stations, clocks and departure conditions.

That gives us a more useful engineering question:

Can a physically supported spacetime configuration allow an arrival that would otherwise be inaccessible within the same elapsed time?

2. Possibility One: Two Mouths of a Wormhole

A wormhole is a proposed connection between different regions of spacetime.

In 1988, physicists Michael Morris and Kip Thorne published mathematical models of wormholes that, under their assumptions, could be traversed by a traveler.

Their work was not a demonstration that a wormhole exists.

It showed that general relativity admits mathematical geometries with features that make traversable passage conceivable.

The difficult part is the material required to maintain the connection.

In the Morris–Thorne models, the throat must remain open without an event horizon blocking passage. In the regular static, spherical Morris–Thorne models, the throat’s flare-out requires violation of the null energy condition. Along a radial light direction at the throat, the radial tension exceeds the local energy density, with both expressed in the same units.

In ordinary language, the model demands properties unlike those of familiar engineering materials.

That is a serious obstacle, but it is not the same as a universal proof that every conceivable wormhole must be impossible.

Could our two devices be wormhole mouths?

If a traversable wormhole already existed, one could imagine associating a device with each mouth.

The devices might serve as navigation stations, instruments, or hypothetical means of controlling the local environment.

But this immediately exposes several unanswered questions.

How would the wormhole be created?

How would its mouths become separated by interstellar distances?

What would keep its throat stable?

Could the required stress-energy be produced and controlled?

And how would a spacecraft pass through without encountering destructive tidal forces or other hazards?

Simply constructing two identical devices at distant locations would not, by itself, establish a wormhole between them.

A connection needs a physical origin, not merely two endpoints.

3. Possibility Two: Shaping the Spacetime Between the Devices

Perhaps the devices would not be wormhole mouths at all.

Instead, could they cooperate to alter the geometry of the region between them?

General relativity relates spacetime curvature to energy and momentum through Einstein's field equations:

Gμν + Λgμν = (8πG/c4)Tμν

The left side describes aspects of spacetime geometry. The right side describes the stress-energy that acts as its source.

This relationship provides a starting point for investigating whether a proposed geometry has a physically plausible source.

But the equations do not say that we can prescribe any desired geometry and then build a machine capable of producing it.

A lesson from warp-drive theory

In 1994, Miguel Alcubierre published a mathematical spacetime construction in which a spacecraft could achieve an effectively superluminal journey relative to distant observers while remaining locally within the light-speed limit.

The construction involved expansion and contraction of space around a traveling region.

It was a theoretical geometry, not an engineered propulsion system.

The original metric requires negative energy density as measured by certain local observers. The prescribed moving geometry does not supply a physical source or a way for the spacecraft to control it.

That distinction is central to our two-device question.

Even if we can calculate a geometry that provides a shorter travel time, we must still determine what creates the geometry, what maintains it, and whether the required physical source is possible.

What could two separated sources accomplish?

This leads to a possible research direction.

Instead of asking whether a single spacecraft carries an entire spacetime-engineering system, we could investigate whether two separated source regions can jointly support a useful geometry.

For example, a theoretical study could examine whether boundary conditions or fields associated with two localized sources admit a consistent spacetime solution.

No solution establishing such a two-device interstellar shortcut is presented here. The proposal is to investigate whether physically admissible solutions exist under explicitly defined assumptions.

We would have to solve for the entire configuration, including the fields and stresses between the devices.

We could not simply assume that the geometry between them takes the desired shape.

And if the devices must first exchange ordinary signals to coordinate, that coordination cannot outrun light through ordinary spacetime.

Any genuinely faster connection would require an additional physical explanation.

4. Possibility Three: A Connection That Changes What Travel Means

There is another important possibility.

Perhaps the useful connection is not created by pushing a spacecraft through a distorted region of otherwise ordinary space.

Instead, it might arise from a more unusual relationship between geometry, quantum fields, and the structure of spacetime.

In 2017, Ping Gao, Daniel Jafferis, and Aron Wall published a theoretical construction involving a particular black-hole geometry with two coupled boundaries.

In their model, an explicit interaction couples the two boundaries of a two-sided anti-de Sitter black hole. The resulting negative averaged null energy changes the geometry and permits signals to cross the pre-existing Einstein–Rosen bridge. The boundary interaction is part of the model.

That is a significant theoretical result.

But it does not describe two ordinary laboratory devices creating an interstellar tunnel.

The model depends on a specialized holographic setting, and its authors explicitly explain that the resulting traversability cannot be used to violate causality.

It demonstrates that the meaning of traversable depends on the physical and mathematical setting.

It does not establish that a practical faster-than-light transportation network can be built.

For our purposes, it offers a useful lesson:

A connection can be mathematically traversable without providing unrestricted faster-than-light travel between ordinary observers.

5. The Problems Two Devices Cannot Simply Avoid

Moving a hypothetical spacetime-engineering system from a spacecraft to two fixed locations might change some engineering questions.

It does not eliminate the underlying physics.

Energy and material requirements

A proposed geometry needs a consistent source.

For certain wormhole and warp-drive geometries, that source violates classical energy conditions.

Quantum physics permits some departures from classical energy conditions, but that does not establish the availability of controllable, macroscopic sources with the properties required by these designs.

Ken Olum showed in 1998 that, under a specific definition of superluminal travel and stated assumptions including a generic condition, such travel requires violation of the weak energy condition.

This is a strong theoretical constraint within its scope, not a proof that every imaginable spacetime construction is impossible.

Stability

A connection that exists mathematically may be unstable.

Matter passing through it could change the geometry. Small disturbances might grow. A configuration that appears acceptable in a static calculation might fail during creation, operation, or shutdown.

Stability must be investigated rather than assumed.

Causality

Relativity connects the ordering of events with the structure of spacetime.

The order assigned to two spacelike-separated events can depend on the choice of clocks and reference frame. A causal violation would require a physical loop, for example a return route that brings a message back to the sender’s own clock before the original departure.

Morris, Thorne, and Ulvi Yurtsever examined how a hypothetical traversable wormhole might be converted into a time machine under particular circumstances.

That does not mean every mathematically traversable connection automatically permits time travel.

It means a proposed connection must be examined for closed causal curves and other possible causality violations.

Creating the connection

This may be the most easily overlooked problem.

Even if a stable connection could exist, how would two devices establish it?

There are three distinct stages to consider:

  1. Creation: What physical process would produce the connection in the first place?
  2. Separation or deployment: If two connected endpoints already existed, how could they be moved to their intended locations while preserving the connection?
  3. Operation: Once established, could signals or spacecraft actually traverse it safely and predictably?

A mathematical solution describing the third stage does not automatically provide a physical mechanism for the first two.

A connection that can be traversed after establishment is not necessarily one that can be created between arbitrary distant locations.

A device at each end is an architectural sketch. If the concept requires prepared infrastructure at both ends, it can address transport between prepared sites only after deployment. Outbound travel, return travel and reuse each require their own checks. Those checks include how moving or accelerating endpoints affect clocks, navigation and the connection’s stability.

6. How Could We Investigate the Idea Scientifically?

The first useful investigation would probably not involve building two machines.

It would involve making the question mathematically precise.

We could begin by defining two source regions, a spacetime background, and a proposed observable.

Then we would ask whether any candidate solution satisfies the relevant physical requirements.

For a meaningful investigation, we would need to establish:

  1. Geometry: What metric or spacetime structure is being proposed?
  2. Sources: What stress-energy produces and maintains it?
  3. Conservation: Does the complete stress-energy, including the devices, fields and their supports, obey local conservation under its own matter equations? Do exchanges and fluxes balance across the chosen boundaries?
  4. Boundaries: How does the proposed region connect to its surroundings?
  5. Causality: Does the construction preserve a consistent causal structure?
  6. Stability: Does it survive small perturbations and passage of a signal or spacecraft?
  7. Observables: What would distinguish the proposed effect from ordinary propagation or measurement error?

A useful negative result might show that a particular two-source geometry cannot satisfy the imposed boundary conditions or source assumptions.

Another might show that the proposed shortcut disappears when the full stress-energy is included.

Those outcomes would still narrow the search.

If a candidate survived the mathematical tests, the next stage would be to identify experimentally accessible consequences.

A physical experiment would require calibrated instrumentation, controls, uncertainty estimates, and a way to distinguish the proposed effect from conventional explanations.

A simulation alone would not establish that the devices work.

BTLB’s WC calculations test signal propagation in a prescribed wormhole geometry. Producing a physical source remains open. WD’s forward mission architecture asks what infrastructure a proposed propulsion mechanism would need after it passes the relevant physics checks. These are separate research tracks. The two-device concept has yet to supply a source model or a predicted signal or vehicle transit.

7. What We Can Say Today

Published general relativity contains mathematical models of traversable wormholes and warp-like geometries.

Published theoretical work also identifies substantial restrictions involving stress-energy, energy conditions, stability, and causality.

Some specialized quantum-gravitational models contain traversable connections without allowing causality violations.

But none of these results demonstrates that two distant engineered devices can establish a controllable shortcut for a spacecraft.

That is the distinction we must preserve.

The two-device idea remains a Beyond the Light Barrier research question—not an adopted physical model, engineering design, or experimental finding.

It might eventually lead to a useful theoretical investigation.

It might reveal a fundamental obstruction.

Or it might help us discover that the right question is not how to connect two distant locations, but which properties of spacetime can actually be controlled by localized physical sources.

For now, the most important next step is not to build the devices.

It is to determine whether the proposed connection can be defined in a way that physics allows us to test.

Two endpoints are easy to imagine. Explaining the spacetime between them is the real challenge.

Sources and Further Reading

  • Morris, M. S., and Thorne, K. S. (1988). Wormholes in spacetime and their use for interstellar travel: A tool for teaching general relativity. American Journal of Physics, 56, 395–412.
  • Morris, M. S., Thorne, K. S., and Yurtsever, U. (1988). Wormholes, Time Machines, and the Weak Energy Condition. Physical Review Letters, 61, 1446–1449.
  • Alcubierre, M. (1994). The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity. Classical and Quantum Gravity, 11, L73–L77.
  • Olum, K. D. (1998). Superluminal Travel Requires Negative Energies. Physical Review Letters, 81, 3567–3570.
  • Gao, P., Jafferis, D. L., and Wall, A. C. (2017). Traversable wormholes via a double trace deformation. Journal of High Energy Physics, 2017, article 151.

Evidence classification: Published speculative theory and a proposed BTLB research question. No new simulation, independent reproduction, or physical experiment is reported.
